### T37. Salt, Brining, and the Dry Brine — Cody's Standing Practice: Heavy, Every Time

<!-- TECHNIQUE-TAGS: meathead, salt, dry-brine, wet-brine, juiciness, myth, roberts-way -->
**Tags:** `meathead` · `salt` · `dry-brine` · `wet-brine` · `juiciness` · `myth` · `roberts-way`
**Source:** **Meathead Goldwyn**, same book and chapter as [§T36](t36-what-meat-actually-is--composition-connective-tissue-and-buying-it-right.md). Reads alongside **[§T29 How to Salt](t29-how-to-salt.md)** (Nosrat) rather than replacing it — where the two overlap they agree; this entry adds Meathead's actual measured numbers and the dry-vs-wet brine science §T29 doesn't cover as specifically.
**Used in:** [§T22 Rib Marinade](t22-rib-marinade--dry-brine-or-wet-marinade-codys-method.md) is Cody's own dry-brine-or-wet-marinade method for ribs, already doing exactly what this entry explains; the rub-cure steps in [§6.2](62-pulled-pork.md), [§6.6](66-north-carolina-pulled-pork-karmel-version.md), and [§6.8](68-memphis-style-beef-ribs.md) are all dry brines by another name.

> **📌 "On the Roberts Way," per Cody: dry brine, heavy, every time.** Not a guess — it's what the numbers below actually favor, and it's why this entry exists rather than staying folded into §T29.

#### Salt types — in practice, you can't taste the difference

Table salt is fine, uniform, usually iodized. Kosher salt (Meathead uses Morton's) has bigger flake grains, no iodine, dissolves slowly — good for pinching and for finishing. Pickling salt has nothing added and dissolves fast in cold water — good for brines. Sea salt is ~99.5% NaCl once refined — fine as a tableside garnish, nothing more. **Curing salts** (Prague Powder #1/#2) are dyed pink and contain nitrite — they fight botulism specifically and are never a table seasoning. **Himalayan pink salt is NOT a curing salt.**

> **Measure salt by weight, not volume.** Grain size changes how much air sits in a spoonful — 1 tsp Morton's Kosher ≈ ½ tsp table salt. A pound of any of them has the same total NaCl.

> ⚠️ **Myth busted: searing seals in the juices.** The crust isn't waterproof — that sizzle is moisture still escaping right through it. Sear anyway, for the browning flavor, not to seal anything.

#### Why brining works — the actual numbers

Salt restructures meat proteins so they **grip water more tightly** under heat. *Cook's Illustrated*: untreated chicken lost 18% of its weight cooking, plain-water-soaked lost 12%, **brined lost only 7%** — and the retained water sits mostly near the surface, exactly where meat dries out first.

**How far salt travels with a wet brine and no heat:** 30 min → ⅒", 1 hr → ¼", 8 hr → ½", 24 hr → ⅔" — **not even a full inch after a full day.**

**Heat moves salt far faster than soaking time does.** Cooked at 230°F: salt reached ⅓" at 100°F internal, ½" at 125°F, ¾" at 145°F, 1" at 160°F. **The real lesson: cooking does most of the distributing, not the wait.**

> ⚠️ **Myth busted: it's osmosis.** Salt is a tiny molecule — it mostly just diffuses through the wide-open cuts, cracks, and capillaries already in the meat. Osmosis only matters once it's already inside the cell.

**The one hard ceiling:** too much salt re-toughens the muscle proteins during cooking — that's the actual thing to watch for, not just "too salty."

#### Dry brine vs. wet brine

| | Dry brine | Wet brine |
|---|---|---|
| Method | salt straight onto the surface, into the fridge | submerge in 5–10% salt water |
| Best for | almost everything — Meathead's own default now | fish, chicken/turkey breasts, pork chops — fast-cooking cuts that would dry out before absorbed water can escape |
| Skip it on | — | fatty cuts (thighs, ribs, shoulder) that don't need the help |
| Poultry skin | **crisps it** | softens and sogs it |
| Amount | ~½ tsp kosher salt (¼ tsp table) per lb — **salt tolerance is personal; treat this as a floor, not a ceiling** | 5–10% salt by weight (1 cup table salt per gallon water ≈ 7.7%) |
| Timing | steaks/chops ~1 hr ahead; roasts overnight to a full day; chicken/turkey at least 2–4 hr, right on the skin | long enough to hit the numbers above — usually overnight |

**Sugar in the brine** (roughly equal to the salt): it can't penetrate more than a fraction of an inch, but it's worth adding anyway — it clings to the surface and pores and helps browning, especially at lower cooking temps.

**Pickling and curing are the same idea, escalated:** pickling brine is stronger and slower (days, since bigger flavor/preservative molecules move in gradually); curing brine adds nitrite/nitrate specifically against botulism (corned beef, bacon, ham, hot dogs) and runs salty enough to actually dehydrate the meat.

> ⚠️ **DOUBLE-SALT JEOPARDY — the one that matters most for going heavy on dry brine.** Commercial rubs are usually already salt-heavy. Brine heavy, then add a salty rub on top, and the two stack into inedible. **Fix: leave salt out of the rub blend and season it separately from the brine**, so it's only ever counted once. Never brine anything already labeled "enhanced"/"basted," and taste before salting any gravy made from brined drippings — salt can be added, never subtracted.

#### On going heavier than Meathead's own ½ tsp/lb — three things worth knowing

1. **Big cuts hide a lot of salt.** Even after 24 hours, salt has moved maybe ⅔" into a brisket or pork butt — most of the interior mass stays unsalted. A heavy surface dose on a 15 lb butt reads far milder on the plate than the same dose on a steak, so going heavier specifically on big smoked cuts is exactly where that instinct pays off. **The instruction that follows from this is the next subsection** — *the salt load scales with the thickness of the cut* — which is the same rule stated from the other end, with Cody's own ribs mistake attached.
2. **The ceiling is toughening, not saltiness** — that's the thing to actually watch for.
3. **A thick fat cap blocks salt almost completely** — on a brisket, the salt is only doing real work where the meat itself is exposed.

#### The salt load scales with the thickness of the cut — heavy on a butt, lighter on ribs

📌 **Cody, 2026-09-14, and this one comes from his own mistake, which is what makes it worth writing down:** *"You want the salt to go into the meat, and so you have to put on a nice heavy coat of salt — especially on a big pork butt. You have to put on a nice heavy coat of salt on a pork butt or brisket… I don't coat it as heavily with ribs because that's a smaller piece of meat, it's a thinner piece of meat and some of it's bone. I still coat it with a nice liberal coat of salt, but **I have gotten ribs too salty because I used the same principle of heavy salt with my pork.** But your pork butts — thick, thick pieces of meat, like a pork butt or a brisket — those get super heavy coats of salt, because you want that salt going all the way into the meat."*

- **Thick cuts — pork butt, brisket — take a very heavy coat.** The salt has a long way to travel and most of the interior mass never sees any of it. **This is item 1 of the list above, turned into an instruction:** even after a full day the salt has moved maybe ⅔" in, so a dose that looks alarming on the outside of a 15 lb butt reads mild on the plate. Not a separate rule — the same one.
- **Ribs take a liberal but noticeably lighter coat.** Thinner meat, less of it, and some of the slab is bone that takes no salt at all — so the same handful that disappears into a butt lands as *too salty* on a rack. **Cody has done exactly that, and says so: he over-salted ribs by carrying the pork-butt instinct across.** That is the useful half of the lesson, and it is why this is written as a warning rather than a preference.
- **The principle, stated generally: the heavy-handed dose is a function of how far the salt has to go, not a universal setting.** Thickness picks the amount, the same way thickness — not weight — picks cooking time ([§T42 What Controls Cooking Time](t42-what-controls-cooking-time.md)). Meathead's ~½ tsp kosher per lb is the floor this cookbook goes heavier than; *how much* heavier is a question about the cut in front of you.
- **Where the ribs half is written up:** [§T22 Rib Marinade — Dry Brine or Wet Marinade (Cody's Method)](t22-rib-marinade--dry-brine-or-wet-marinade-codys-method.md), Method 1 Step 1. ⚠️ **It does not override a printed quantity in a transcribed recipe** — [§7.97 Last-Meal Ribs](797-last-meal-ribs.md) says **½ teaspoon per pound** because its source page says so, and that stays exactly as printed.

#### Uncovered, on a rack — the standing rule for every dry brine in this book

📌 **Cody, 2026-09-13:** *"The uncovered salt-brining, dry-brine phase — you leave it in the fridge uncovered on a rack. All you have to say is so that the meat is exposed to air on all sides… I just think — so that it's exposed to the air on all sides, and it's sitting on a rack, or a grill rack, or whatever that thing's called."*

**Dry-brined meat goes uncovered, on a rack, so air reaches every side of it — not just the top.** A rack — a cooling rack, a roasting rack, a grill grate set over a sheet pan, whatever fits — lifts the meat off the pan so air circulates underneath too, not only over the top.

**Why — the salt first; the bark is the last thing on this list, not the first.**

> ✏️ **Corrected 2026-09-14 on Cody's own account, and the correction is the point.** From 2026-09-13 this paragraph led with the bark and said the open air *"lets the meat take a real bark or crisp skin instead of steaming."* **That put a secondary effect first and borrowed the word *steaming* from a rule about searing that has nothing to do with a fridge-stage dry brine.** His account below replaces it; the four items are in his order of importance, not the old one.

**1. Salt travels toward moisture, and the moisture is inside the meat.** Cody, 2026-09-14: *"The real behavior of the salt — it's not osmosis, it's something else. It's similar to osmosis, but it's where the salt wants to go to moisture. And so if you leave it open to the air on the outside, the salt will want to go into the meat because there's moisture in the meat."* **Leaving the surface open to the air is what keeps that direction of travel going — the salt goes *in*.** And **his description and Meathead's are the same phenomenon**: the ⚠️ **Myth busted: it's osmosis** note a few paragraphs up, under "Why brining works — the actual numbers," already busts that exact word — *salt is a tiny molecule; it mostly just diffuses through the wide-open cuts, cracks, and capillaries already in the meat.* Read it there rather than re-derived here. He arrived at "it's not osmosis" independently, and the book agrees with him.

**2. Once inside, the salt restructures the proteins so they hold onto water during the cook.** **Cody's description, in his own words:** *"when the salt does that, it starts creating little pockets as it disrupts some of the proteins as I understand it. In those little pockets, when the cooking process happens, it holds moisture, and it'll hold the juice in those pockets, actually making the whole thing more tender."* **This entry's own sourced line says the same thing in Meathead's terms** — *salt restructures meat proteins so they **grip water more tightly** under heat* — with the *Cook's Illustrated* retention numbers already above (untreated lost 18% of its weight cooking, plain-water-soaked 12%, **brined only 7%**). ⚠️ **The "little pockets" is Cody's lay description of a real mechanism, not a published finding, and this entry is not asserting it as one.** Two ways of describing one thing: his, and the sourced one. Where they need to be told apart — a rewrite, a dispute, a number — the Meathead line and the *Cook's Illustrated* figures are the citable half.

**3. The interior ends up seasoned, not just the surface.** This is the payoff Cody cares about most, and it is worth saying plainly: *"when the salt goes into the meat, the interior of the meat also tastes seasoned, and it's very nice. So you have a salty meat throughout the meat, not just on the surface. It makes a huge difference."* Surface salt seasons a crust; salt that has had a night to travel seasons the bite.

**4. And then, secondary: the bark.** He affirms this part explicitly — *"your statement about getting a bark is true. The outside, the very exterior, if you leave it open to air, it will dry. And then when you put mustard and then a seasoning on it, it will turn into a nice chewy bark. That's very true. I'm not arguing with you there."* A dried exterior takes a slather and a rub better and builds a chewier bark, which is the same physical argument [§T39 Maillard vs. Caramelization](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md) makes about keeping the surface dry for browning. **Real, but fourth on this list — not the reason the rack is in the rule.**

> **What this is *not*: the pat-dry-before-searing rule. Cody drew that line himself, and it is the reason the old wording was wrong.** In his words: *"the whole steam thing — this situation is different than patting the meat completely dry, which is one of the most important steps before you sear. That's apples and oranges, because you're not searing things here. We're talking about a low and slow cook typically when you dry brine."* **Two different rules, two different cooks.** The obsessive towel-dry immediately before a hot sear ([§3 Darcy's Steak](3-darcys-steak.md) Steps 4–5, [§T39](t39-maillard-vs-caramelization--gbd.md)'s *keep the surface dry*) is about the seconds before a screaming pan or a chimney. A dry brine on a rack is a fridge stage ahead of a long, low cook. Don't let one borrow the other's vocabulary.

**Does this apply to steaks? — answering Cody's own hedge, since the book already answers it.** He hedged: *"I'm not gonna say you can't dry brine steaks — I've done it before, and it might even be recommended in Meathead's book. If it is, then just ignore me here."* **It is, and it's already in this entry.** The dry-brine-vs-wet-brine table above has it in the Timing row: ***steaks/chops ~1 hr ahead***; roasts overnight to a full day. So **dry brining steaks is Meathead's own practice, at about an hour ahead** — nothing to ignore. **But the rack-and-open-air rule above is aimed at the long brines** — the overnight-to-a-full-day ones on big smoked cuts, which is what Cody was describing — and a one-hour steak salt is a different thing at a different scale. **Do not read this subsection as "every steak needs an overnight uncovered rack."** And to be straight about the limit of the evidence: **the table's Timing row says *when*, not *how*. It does not itself specify uncovered-on-a-rack for the one-hour steak case, and this cookbook is not inventing that claim** *(per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md) — judgment fills gaps, it does not invent facts).*

This is a fridge-stage rule specifically — a wet brine (submerged) obviously doesn't need a rack — and it doesn't change anything about brine strength, timing, or the salt-type guidance above.
